subject: stan model I made after reading "Bayesian Model-Building by Pure Thought"

messages.author: 52c2b686b48e3db4
messages.subject: stan model I made after reading "Bayesian Model-Building by Pure Thought"
parts:
Hi everyone,

I was reading a paper that Andrew linked to in a recent post, about wanting models to be insensitive to the scale of discretization. As one example, he describes (section 3) fitting a function that's constrained to be increasing, and how you'll really be led astray by a prior that's uniform over the function values at discrete points (with a restriction that the values are increasing). As the number of points in the discretization increases, the mass of the prior concentrates around a straight line, which is bad.

Just for fun, I thought about how I might approach this problem, and then coded the model in Stan. I imagine that my approach is either wrong, or is old hat to you folks. But I'm writing to this group about it because:

1. I'm very new to Stan (etc.), so if anyone has any feedback (on either the Stan model or how I decided to think about the problem), I'd really appreciate it. 
2. Maybe something here (the approach, the model, the R code) will be interesting or useful to one of you? I'm very new to Stan, so I don't know what's interesting vs. trivial to people.

So here's how I thought about it:

The function  mu  increases from 0 at time 0 to some unknown value at time 1, with discrete intermediate values  mu[i]  (where  i  represents the discretization and ranges from  1  to  N). Each data point  y[i]  is drawn from a normal distribution centered on  mu[i].   

I modeled the jumps as chi-squared-distributed. This is nice since 1 jump that's distributed as chi-squared(k)  is then equivalent to  n  independent jumps that are distributed as  chi-squared(k/N). Then our prior for the function  mu  is independent of the scale of the discretization if we express it in terms of  k_0, where the sum of all the jumps (which is  mu[N]  ) is distributed as  chi-squared(k_0). Similarly, the variance of the  y's  should scale with  1/N, since I'm assuming that the  y's  at a coarser scale are an average of the y's at a finer scale.  So the model is:

(For i in 1:N):

mu_i ~ mu_{i-1} + s*chi_square(k_0/N)   (mu_0 = 0)  
y_y ~ N(mu_i, sqrt(sigma_0_sq*N))

(The parameter  s  lets us vary both the size and variance of the jumps. Maybe it would have been better to express the model explicitly in terms of the jump size/variance independently.)

You can see my Stan code and R code on Github here.

In the plots (attached and on Github), you can see me doing what Andrew suggested in that paper: I fit the model (using simulated data) at two different levels of aggregation. The  y's  at the coarser scale are an average of the  y's  at the finer scale. Plotting the posterior means of  mu  for each model, we can see that the estimated function is similar for the two different discretizations, which is what we would hope for. I also plotted samples from the posterior from the two models, and they look pretty similar.

A better model (hierarchical) would (instead of assuming they're known) put a prior on the hyperparameters (k_0, s, sigma_0_sq). But I decided to start from here.

I'd love to hear what you think!

Thanks,

-David
